title: Ulysses
author: James Joyce
openingText: Stately, plump Buck Mulligan came from the stairhead, bearing a bowl of lather on which a mirror and a razor lay crossed. A yellow dressinggown, ungirdled, was sustained gently behind him by the mild morning air.
about:
Ulysses is one day in the life of Leopold Bloom, a Jewish advertising salesman in Dublin — June 16, 1904. The novel follows him from breakfast through funeral, work, lunch, library, pub, brothel, and home in eighteen episodes, each in a different style. Around Bloom is Stephen Dedalus, the young writer, and Bloom's wife Molly, whose monologue closes the book.

James Joyce published Ulysses in 1922, after years of work. The novel maps onto Homer's Odyssey episode by episode, with Bloom as Odysseus and Stephen as Telemachus. It is the most famous experimental novel in English and arguably the founding work of modernism.

angleCards.title: The formal experiment, episode by episode.
angleCards.text: Joyce reinvents his narrative technique for each of the eighteen episodes — interior monologue, catechism, newspaper parody, operatic libretto. I want to read Ulysses as a laboratory, noticing how each stylistic choice shapes what we know and feel about the same characters.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to read episode by episode, following Joyce's formal experiment — how he changes the narrative technique with each chapter, and what each style reveals that the others couldn't.

angleCards.title: Bloom as the modern Odysseus.
angleCards.text: Homer's hero was cunning, brave, and exceptional. Joyce's hero buys a pork kidney. I want to read the Homeric parallels carefully — understanding what Joyce gains by mapping epic onto the mundane, and whether Bloom's decency is a form of heroism the ancient world couldn't have named.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to read Leopold Bloom as the modern hero — understanding what it means that Joyce's Odysseus runs a newspaper ad and makes breakfast, and whether ordinariness is heroism in a different key.

angleCards.title: The father and the son.
angleCards.text: Stephen Dedalus is young, brilliant, and homeless in spirit. Leopold Bloom lost his son Rudy as an infant and has never recovered. Their paths converge on June 16 in a way that feels inevitable and doesn't resolve into anything neat. I want to follow what passes between them.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to follow the relationship between Stephen and Bloom — what each lacks that the other has, and whether their brief meeting amounts to something like the father-son bond neither of them has.

angleCards.title: Bloomsday as real autobiography.
angleCards.text: June 16, 1904 was the day James Joyce first walked out with Nora Barnacle — the woman he loved for the rest of his life. He chose it deliberately. I want to read the novel with that biographical key in hand, understanding what Joyce was doing by immortalising a particular Thursday in Dublin.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to read June 16 as a real day — understanding the biographical fact that it was Joyce's first walk with Nora Barnacle, and what it means that he chose to make it the most scrutinised day in literary history.

cast.name: Leopold Bloom
cast.description: A Dublin advertising canvasser of Hungarian-Jewish descent. Practical, curious, kind, and quietly grieving. He is Joyce's Odysseus — making his way through the city of Dublin on a single Thursday, doing ordinary things with extraordinary inner life.

cast.name: Stephen Dedalus
cast.description: A young schoolteacher and failed poet, newly returned from Paris and still in mourning for his mother. Brilliant, proud, and spiritually homeless. He is Telemachus looking for a father he can't name yet.

cast.name: Molly Bloom
cast.description: A professional singer having an affair with her concert promoter. The novel closes with her unpunctuated interior monologue — 45 pages of unbroken thought that ends with the most famous "yes" in literature.

cast.name: Buck Mulligan
cast.description: A medical student of brilliant, corrosive wit. He opens the novel. His mockery of everything, including Stephen, is funny and destructive in equal measure. Joyce based him on his real friend Oliver St. John Gogarty.

cast.name: Blazes Boylan
cast.description: Molly's concert promoter and, on this particular afternoon, her lover. Bloom knows. The knowledge sits in him all day. Boylan appears briefly but casts a long shadow over every scene Bloom navigates.

cast.name: The City of Dublin
cast.description: Dublin on June 16, 1904, rendered in extraordinary topographic detail. Streets, pubs, churches, the sea at Sandymount. The city is as much a character as any person — specific, alive, and the ground on which everything else happens.

acclaim.quote: I hold this book to be the most important expression which the present age has found.

whyItMatters.title: One Day, Eighteen Styles
whyItMatters.body: The novel spends each episode in a different prose register — newspaper headlines, catechism, parody of medieval English, stream of consciousness. The form argues that a single day in a single city contains every register a writer could use.

whyItMatters.title: Ordinary Heroism
whyItMatters.body: Where Homer's Odysseus is a king and warrior, Bloom is an ad salesman with a difficult marriage. The book proposes that the same patterns of Homeric heroism — wandering, return, recognition — can be found in an ordinary day. Most modern fiction has worked from this premise since.

whyItMatters.title: The Final Monologue
whyItMatters.body: Molly Bloom's closing chapter is one paragraph, eight long sentences, almost no punctuation. It is the most-quoted passage in modernist literature. Reading it is encountering the book's argument that consciousness is not what novels had assumed it was.
